name: Koshin
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Ousmanou (2014) How to Disclose the Environment through Linguistic Description: A Basic Linguistic Analysis of Koshin [Beboid Bantu, Cameroon], 462 pp. grammar (Glottolog langdoc)

new_statements.quote: The vocalic sounds discussed thus far do not occur alone within the syllable structure. They appear with prosodic units called tones. In fact, like the vast majority of African languages, Koshin shows a prosodic contrast of tones. Beside tones, other prosodic units are attested: the prosodies of labialization and coronalization (palatalization). Nasalization prosody is also attested. [...] Koshin language shows three level tones, which are usually carried by vowels but sometimes by nasal consonants. Some falling and rising tones are attested. But they are regarded as mere association of level tones. [...] (p.108) The syllable and the prosodic word domains (on a par with the “foot” in languages where it is relevant) are considered minor prosodic constituents
new_statements.citation: Ousmanou. 2014. How to Disclose the Environment through Linguistic Description: A Basic Linguistic Analysis of Koshin ["Beboid" Bantu, Cameroon]. PhD dissertation, Université de Yaoundé I.
new_statements.locator: Ch.2 §2.2-2.2.1.1, p.43 (PDF p.61); minimal pairs §2.2.1.4 p.45; foot remark ch.5 §5.2 p.108 (PDF p.126)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koshin is described as a tone language with three contrastive level tones (H, M, L; contours = sequences of levels), tone having both lexical and grammatical (e.g. cl.9/10 sg/pl) function. The 444-page grammar enumerates the language's prosodic units as tone, labialization, palatalization and (phrasal) nasalization and never mentions word stress or accent; the only nod is that the metrical foot is a constituent 'in languages where it is relevant', implicitly not Koshin. No statement of stress position exists in the primary description.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The grammar does document stem-initial positional privilege (labialization/coronalization affect only the onset of the first syllable of the prosodic word, pp.74-75; in disyllabic verb roots the second syllable admits only the vowels a/ə and is the only place L tone occurs, p.152), the same kind of evidence Lovegren 2012 analyses as abstract stem-initial accent in neighbouring Mungbam, but Ousmanou does not draw that conclusion.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prosody = tone; the only 'prominence' discussed is phonological-phrase-level (NP head at left edge of the phonological phrase, pp.115-116), not word stress. Data are citation forms and elicited phrases from Koshin village.
new_statements.identity_note: Ousmanou 2014 describes the speech of Koshin village (Fungom subdivision, Menchum, NW Region), i.e. kosh1246 proper (Glottolog groups it with Bukwen as Koshin-Bukwen kosh1247). Lovegren 2012 is about Mungbam (abar1238/mung1266 area), cited only as areal context.

sources.note: Nothing. Ch.2 §2.2 'Prosodic Units' (pp.43-46) lists the prosodic units as tone (three contrastive level tones H, M, L; lexical and grammatical function) plus labialization/palatalization prosodies and phrasal nasalization; ch.4-5 treat syllable, prosodic word, phonological/intonational phrase. The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur as phonological terms in 462 pages; p.108 remarks that the foot is a prosodic constituent only 'in languages where it is relevant'.
